html:
Akhenaten was a pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty, in the New Kingdom, who reigned for about seventeen years in the mid-1300s BCE. He tried to replace Egypt's many gods with the worship of one, the Aten, the disc of the sun.

He came to the throne as Amenhotep IV, son of Amenhotep III. In his fifth year he changed his name to Akhenaten, "effective for the Aten", and began Atenism. The temples of Amun, the great god of Thebes, lost their funds, and Amun's name was hacked off monuments. He built a new capital on empty desert ground at Amarna, called Akhetaten, "horizon of the Aten".

His reign changed art. Statues and reliefs showed the king with a long face, thin neck and wide hips, and showed the royal family at home, kissing and playing with their daughters, under the rays of the sun. His queen Nefertiti was unusually prominent; her painted bust, found at Amarna, is one of the best known works of ancient art. Clay letters found there, the Amarna letters, record his dealings with the kings of Babylon, Mitanni and the Hittites, and pleas for help from his vassals in Canaan.

After his death the old gods returned. His probable son Tutankhamun changed his own name from Tutankhaten and left Amarna. Later kings abandoned the city and struck Akhenaten from the king lists as a heretic. Historians still argue whether his faith was true monotheism.
